paper.title: The Stag Hunt and the Evolution of Social Structure

headline: Stag Hunt (agent-based): 3/3 locked clauses REPRO; canonical x*_emp=0.675 (analytic 0.667); risk-dominant Hare basin P=0.692 > Stag P=0.308; threshold tracks payoff formula (worst |err|=0.025)

verdicts.gate: P1 bistable basin threshold at predicted interior fixed point (x*_emp in [0.62,0.72]; all-Stag rare below x*, near-certain above)
P2 risk-dominant Hare owns the strictly larger basin (P(fixate Hare) = 0.667 +- 0.05 AND > P(fixate Stag))
P3 threshold TRACKS the payoff formula (x*_emp within +-0.05 of analytic x* for {0.667, 0.500, 0.200}, not a fixed 50/50)

extra.scope: faithful reproduction of a published coordination-game model; no real-world data; the contribution is whether the harness + discipline reproduce the BISTABLE two-basin equilibrium selection (payoff-dominant vs risk-dominant), show the risk-dominant basin is larger, and confirm the separatrix tracks the analytic payoff formula, and would catch an artifact

citations: Skyrms, B. (2004). The Stag Hunt and the Evolution of Social Structure. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139165228.
Maynard Smith, J. & Price, G.R. (1973). The logic of animal conflict. Nature 246:15-18.
Schlag, K.H. (1998). Why imitate, and if so, how? A boundedly rational approach to multi-armed bandits. J. Economic Theory 78(1):130-156.

benchmark.note: no cross-tool baseline; faithful single-implementation reproduction graded against the empirical basin separatrix x*_emp, the risk-dominant fixation probability, and the analytic interior fixed point x*=(P-S_)/((R-T)+(P-S_))
